papers.title: Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction for Generalized Anxiety Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) for anxiety symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Design: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Data Sources: CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Scopus, SocINDEX, ERIC (EBSCO), and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global were searched from inception to October 2025; identified trial protocols were hand-searched for subsequent reports through February 2026. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies: Randomized, non-randomized, and single-arm trials evaluating the effects of MBSR on anxiety in adults with GAD. Data extraction and synthesis: Two authors independently screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. The primary outcome was anxiety symptoms; the secondary outcome was adverse events. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted, and certainty of evidence was assessed. Results: Of 19 included reports (16 independent samples), 8 randomized controlled trials (n=1,012) were included in the primary meta-analysis. MBSR significantly reduced anxiety symptoms vs. waitlist (Hedges' g=-0.88; 95% CI -1.57 to -0.19) and general active comparators (g=-0.85; 95% CI -1.15 to -0.54), and showed no significant difference vs. escitalopram in two linked trials (g=0.09; 95% CI -0.11 to 0.29), with fewer adverse events in the in-person trial, the only one reporting them (15% vs. 79%; number needed to treat to avoid harm=2). GRADE certainty of evidence was high for the escitalopram comparison and very low for waitlist. Conclusions: MBSR is a well-tolerated, nonpharmacologic treatment option for adults with GAD. Anxiety reductions were similar to escitalopram, with fewer adverse events; independent replication is needed. MBSR may be a viable option for patients who prefer non-pharmacological management or who cannot tolerate medication. Systematic review registration: PROSPERO CRD420251140213.

papers.title: The Effect of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy on Kinesiophobia in Older Adults with Chronic Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To determine the effect of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy on kinesiophobia in older adults with chronic knee osteoarthritis. PATIENTS AND METHODS: This randomized clinical trial conducted among 56 older patients with knee osteoarthritis at health centers in Kashan, Iran, in 2024. Participants were selected via consecutive sampling and randomly assigned to either an intervention (n = 28) or a control (n = 28) group using block randomization. The intervention group participated in eight 90 minute sessions of Mindfulness Based Cognitive Therapy, while the control group received routine care. Kinesiophobia was measured with the Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia (TSK11) at baseline, week 4 (immediately post intervention), and week 8 (four week follow up). Covariate adjusted repeated measures ANCOVA was performed, adjusting for age, number of children, and baseline pain intensity. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. All participants completed follow up. RESULTS: The mean kinesiophobia score decreased from 29.46 ± 3.81 at baseline to 25.68 ± 3.22 at week 8 in the intervention group and from 28.64 ± 4.78 to 26.68 ± 5.15 in the control group. The adjusted repeated-measures analysis showed a significant group-by-time interaction (Wilks' Λ = 0.88, F(2.50) = 3.34, p = 0.040, ηp CONCLUSION: Four weeks of MBCT may influence the trajectory of kinesiophobia over time in older adults with knee osteoarthritis. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20231105059961N1).

papers.title: Exploring the effects of mindfulness meditation on resting-state functional connectivity: an overview.
papers.abstract: Mindfulness meditation has received growing interest in research over the past decades. Mindfulness meditation training (MMT) can be employed as a mental practice to improve cognitive skills such as attention and emotion regulation and may promote well-being. Neuroimaging studies have emerged to understand the effects of MMT on brain functioning. However, no review exists on the effects of MMT on resting-state brain functional connectivity (rsFC) in healthy meditation-naïve adults specifically. We, therefore, aimed to provide an overview of studies that investigated the effects of MMT on rsFC in healthy meditation-naïve adults, as well as their link to cognitive and clinical measures. Several studies reported changes in MMT-induced rsFC within and between regions of the default mode (DMN), salience (SN), and central executive (CEN) networks. Both increases and decreases in rsFC have been observed for brain regions associated with these networks after MMT, each with differential roles in emotion regulation, stress, and cognitive functions. Some studies highlighted associations between changes in rsFC after MMT and modifications in cognitive performance and psycho-affective measures, which may be influenced by MMT-specific characteristics such as practice duration or delivery methods. MMT may induce a reorganization in the brain's functional architecture by altering rsFC within and between these networks and seems to modify processes related to attention, executive memory, emotional regulation, stress, and resilience. Investigating functional connectivity during rest in key brain networks seems a promising approach to understand the effects of mindfulness meditation on overall well-being.

papers.title: Developing a digital heart failure symptom management intervention using the preparation phase of the Multiphase Optimization StraTegy.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Persons with heart failure (HF) often experience bothersome symptoms in daily life, which can negatively affect their health-related quality of life (HRQOL). Self-care e.g. to monitor and manage symptoms, is essential in HF management. Self-care can stabilize the disease, reduce symptoms, and improve outcomes. However, patients often find it difficult to recognize and manage symptoms due to various factors. Consequently, many people delay acting until their symptoms become too severe to manage by themselves. This highlights the need for timely engagement in symptom monitoring and interpretation to enable early and appropriate responses. In the SympTom mAnagement and self-caRe (STAR) study, we prepare (phase 1), optimize (phase 2), and evaluate (phase 3) a digital intervention using the Multiphase Optimization StraTegy (MOST). The STAR intervention supports patients with HF in recognizing their symptoms and taking timely, appropriate actions. OBJECTIVE: The aim of this study is to describe the MOST preparation phase of the STAR intervention, including its development of the underlying conceptual model, identification of candidate components and optimization criterion, and assessment of intervention feasibility to inform the subsequent optimization phase. METHODS: We conducted four sequential activities from the preparation phase of MOST: (1) developing a conceptual model; (2) identifying candidate components; (3) identifying optimization criterion; and (4) conducting a feasibility study of the digital STAR intervention with patients with HF and HF nurses. RESULTS: The conceptual model includes four candidate components; a basic component, symptom awareness training, symptom management counselling, and symptom management experiments. We expect these components to influence behavioral outcomes such as reduced symptom burden and hospitalizations, and improved self-care and HRQOL. The set of candidate components were specified at two levels (low versus high) by varying intensity, frequency, or mode of delivery while maintaining consistent core content. Ten patients with HF and 5 HF nurses tested the STAR intervention in the feasibility study. The STAR intervention was perceived as feasible from both a patient and nurses' perspective. Patients rated the intervention as clear, user-friendly and structured. Participants valued personal support from HF nurses and perceived it as important for continued use of the intervention. The feasibility findings provide concrete input to refine the intervention prior to the optimization trial. CONCLUSION: The STAR intervention is feasible and acceptable to both patients with HF and HF nurses. Combined with the conceptual model, linking components to underlying mechanisms and outcomes, the findings provide us a solid foundation for optimizing the STAR intervention in a subsequent optimization trial.

papers.title: Common Phenomenal and Neural Substrate Geometry in Visual Motion Perception.
papers.abstract: What is a possible physical substrate of the qualitative aspects of consciousness (qualia)? Answering this question is a central goal of consciousness research. Due to their subjective and ineffable nature, finding a quantitative way to characterise qualia from verbal description has thus far proven elusive. To overcome the challenge of expressing subjective experience, recent structural and relational approaches have been proposed from mathematics. Yet, as far as we know, no attempts have been made to evaluate the relationship between a certain structure of qualia and the structure of a candidate underlying physical substrate. Towards this ambitious goal of linking the structures of qualia and physical, we set out to make an empirical first step by focusing on experienced dissimilarity of visual motion in human participants and stimulus-evoked neural population response geometry recorded from mouse primary visual cortex. From human participants (N=171), we obtained dissimilarity ratings of visual motion experiences induced by 48 stimuli, spanning across 8 directions and 6 spatial frequencies. Analysis revealed a human dissimilarity structure that was not well captured by a simple monotonic function of physical motion-direction difference alone nor by a pure orientation-symmetry account. From nine individual mice, we recorded single-neuron activity (n=751) with optical imaging in both awake and lightly anaesthetised conditions (isoflurane 0.6-0.8%). From neuron population responses to a similar set of motion stimuli, we computed a distance matrix that is comparable to our human dissimilarity matrix. Quantitative analyses show structural commonalities between a human dissimilarity structure and mouse neural structure, where a categorical organisation of stimulus direction best explained both. These commonalities were similar in awake and anaesthetised recordings, suggesting that this coarse V1 geometry is relatively insensitive to this type of anaesthesia; future work combining behaviour with causal intervention is required to relate such neural structures to conscious experience. Finally, we list several empirical factors that can be improved to promote our qualia structure approach in the future.

papers.title: Influence of Preoperative Virtual Reality on Preoperative State Anxiety in the Ambulatory Setting: The AMBLUMEEN Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative anxiety affects 30% to 80 % of ambulatory surgery patients and is associated with increased anesthetic requirements, postoperative pain, and delayed recovery. Virtual reality (VR) is a promising nonpharmacological anxiolytic, but evidence remains limited in the ambulatory setting. METHODS: The AMBLUMEEN (AMBulatory LUMEEN) trial is a single-center, randomized, open-label, superiority trial conducted in an adult ambulatory surgery unit. Patients with moderate-to-severe preoperative anxiety (State-Trait Anxiety Inventory Form Y-A [STAI-YA] > 45) were randomized 1:1 to standard care alone (control) or standard care and a single 20-minute preoperative VR session (immersive 360° natural contemplative scenes). The primary end point was the change in STAI-YA score from arrival in the ambulatory unit (baseline) to immediately before operating room transfer (presurgery), analyzed under the intention-to-treat principle with a linear mixed model. Secondary end points included preoperative benzodiazepine use, postoperative morphine requirement, unplanned overnight admission, patient satisfaction, and device acceptability. RESULTS: Of 106 randomized patients (53 per group) with a median [interquartile range] baseline STAI-YA of 49 [46-55] and 49 [46-58] respectively in the control and VR group, the VR group experienced a markedly greater reduction in state anxiety than controls. Adjusted mean between-group difference in STAI-YA change from baseline to presurgery was -18.7 95% confidence interval (CI) [-21.4 to -16.1] points in favor of VR. Although benzodiazepine requirement, postoperative pain, and unplanned overnight admission were comparable between groups, the morphine requirement in postanesthesia care unit was lower in the VR group (6/53 [11.3% 95% CI, 11.3 {4.3-23.0}] vs 0/53 [0.0%, 95% CI, {0.0-6.7}]; P = .027). Global perioperative satisfaction was high in both groups (median 8 [8-9] on 10). CONCLUSIONS: A single 20-minute session of medical-grade VR significantly reduced preoperative anxiety in ambulatory surgery patients, with high acceptability and an excellent safety profile.

papers.title: Implicit Self-Death Associations and Symptoms of Depression and Anxiety: A Single-Case Experimental Design.
papers.abstract: Death anxiety may operate as a transdiagnostic process underlying anxiety and depressive symptoms. This study used the Death-Implicit Association Task (D-IAT) to index implicit self-death associations (ISDA) and evaluated a brief mindfulness intervention using a concurrent multiple-baseline design with maintenance across four students with prior anxiety/depressive diagnoses. Across 20 daily sessions, D-IAT D-scores and Mini-DASS depression and anxiety scores were collected. articles.title: Did Substack Fix the Internet?
articles.excerpt: A new book by Hamish McKenzie, the platform’s co-founder, argues that writers today are more empowered than ever. But online newsletters form their own kind of attention economy.
